title: Signals or Messages: Why "Can We Talk?" Ruins a Weekend
summary: Vague messages feel safe to send and land as worry. What Zaleznik meant by signals and messages, what uncertainty does to stress, and how to write the clear version.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Friday, 5:47 p.m. A DM from your manager: "Can we find time to talk on Monday?" No agenda, no topic. They've already closed the laptop and headed to dinner. You spend the weekend running through every conversation it could possibly be. By Monday you've lived through three imaginary versions, two of them bad. Then the meeting turns out to be about moving the sprint review to Thursday.

Most of us have sent a message like that, and most of us have received one. This post is about why one vague line can eat someone's whole weekend, and what the clear version looks like.

A signal and a message

The two words come from Abraham Zaleznik's 1977 Harvard Business Review essay "Managers and Leaders: Are They Different?". He described managers who talk to their teams indirectly, "using 'signals' instead of 'messages.'" In his words, "A signal holds a number of implicit positions, while a message clearly states a position." A signal stays open to reinterpretation if people get upset. A message carries the risk that "some people will indeed not like what they hear" (Zaleznik, HBR).

"Can we talk?" is a signal. "Can I grab 15 minutes on Monday to go over the API design? Nothing about your performance, I'd just like a second pair of eyes" is a message. Each takes the sender about ten seconds to type. They cost the receiver two very different weekends.

Why signals feel safer to send

Hardly anyone sends signals to be mean. A signal feels safe. It commits to nothing. It puts off the awkward part, leaves room for "I never said that," and skips the feelings for now. Zaleznik saw the same pattern: a direct message raises the emotional temperature, and that "makes managers anxious."

So the manager who keeps the budget vague, or explains a decision halfway, often believes they're sparing the team some worry. Usually they're sparing themselves a hard five minutes. The care is real. It's just aimed at the wrong person.

The cost moves to the receiver

The discomfort of a hard conversation doesn't go away when you send a signal. It moves. The sender skips it, and the receiver pays it back with interest, one worst-case rehearsal at a time.

A lab study from University College London shows why this hurts so much. Forty-five volunteers played a computer game where they turned over rocks that might hide a snake, and a snake meant a mildly painful shock on the hand. The odds kept changing. Self-reported stress, pupil size and sweating all tracked how uncertain people were. A 50% chance of a shock was the most stressful situation, and 0% or 100% were the least (de Berker et al., 2016; UCL summary). The lead author put it simply: "it's much worse not knowing you are going to get a shock than knowing you definitely will or won't." A Slack DM is not an electric shock. Still, "Can we talk?" is a very effective way to park someone at 50/50 for two days.

Spread that across a team and you get a constant background hum under the work: people reading tone, checking who got invited to which meeting, bracing against vagueness that usually wasn't meant as a threat at all. None of that energy goes into the product.

How vagueness grows office politics

A team that can't count on clear messages learns to get by without them. People start reading signals everywhere: the wording of a reorg note, who replied and who went silent, whose name came first on the invite. Information turns into something to hold onto and interpret instead of something to share. Zaleznik wrote about this too, about "the veils of ambiguity and signaling so characteristic of managerial cultures."

That's how a manager ends up seen as distant, hard to read, even scheming, when the real story is someone who kept dodging direct conversations. From inside the team, the politics make sense: it's how people cope with a gap where clear messages should be. Fill the gap and a lot of the maneuvering dies down on its own. If politics is already part of your week, this post on office politics picks up from here.

Clear is kind, especially when it's hard

Think of two doctors. One says "we should run some tests" and walks out. The other says "this looks like a sprain. Here's what we'll do, and here's the one sign that would worry me." The second one gives you more information, some of it unwelcome, and you still leave feeling better, because you have something solid to hold instead of a blank to fill with your worst guesses.

Hard news at work follows the same rule. "This part isn't working, here's specifically why, and here's what I'd like us to try" is harder to say than "we should chat sometime." It's also much easier to hear. Kim Scott's Radical Candor has a name for the soft trap: Ruinous Empathy, when you care about someone but hold back or "sugar-coat it" (Radical Candor). Vague feels kind to send and lands as worry. Clear feels hard to send and, more often than you'd expect, lands as respect.

Signal in, message out

Signal Message
"Can we talk?" "Can I get 15 minutes on Monday about the API design? Nothing about your performance."
"Let's take this offline." "I don't want to hold up the meeting. Can we do 10 minutes right after, about the rollout date?"
"Some people have concerns about the release." "Two people on support are worried about the migration step. Could you reply in their thread before Thursday?"
"We're making some changes to the team." "From next sprint, the payments work moves to another team. Your role stays the same. Let's go through it at 2 today."
"Interesting approach." (on a PR) "I think this breaks retries when the call times out. Can we add a test for that case?"

The real test is when things are tense

Clear messages are easy when nothing is at stake. The test comes with bad news, a disagreement, a missed deadline, someone upset in the room. That's exactly when people slide back into signals: the vague reschedule, "let's take this offline," feedback softened until it says nothing at all.

Clear is also different from blunt. Radical Candor calls the blunt version Obnoxious Aggression: "You challenge, but you don't show you care." Bluntness makes the moment about the sender's frustration. What you want is a message that's clear and kind at once, sent right when clarity is hardest to give. For a step-by-step version of that conversation, try this script for difficult feedback.

Try this week

  • Before you send "can we talk?", add the topic, how long it'll take and whether anything is wrong.
  • Pick one vague update you've been sitting on and say it plainly.
  • When you receive a signal, ask for the message: "Sure. What's it about, so I can prep?"
  • If you have to delay a decision, say when you'll make it.

This is the third post in the leadership series. Next up: staying with a problem you can't solve yet.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a signal and a message?
faqs.a: The terms come from Abraham Zaleznik's 1977 Harvard Business Review essay. A message clearly states a position. A signal holds several implicit positions and stays open to reinterpretation. "Can we talk?" is a signal. "Can I get 15 minutes on Monday about the API design? Nothing about your performance" is a message.

faqs.q: Why do managers send vague signals?
faqs.a: Mostly to protect themselves. A signal commits to nothing, delays the awkward part and leaves room to say "I never said that." Zaleznik noted that direct messages raise emotions and make managers anxious. The vagueness often feels kind to the sender, but the receiver ends up carrying the worry.

faqs.q: Why does a vague message cause so much stress?
faqs.a: Uncertainty itself is stressful. In a 2016 University College London study, volunteers in a game with mild electric shocks were most stressed when the chance of a shock was 50%, and least stressed at 0% or 100%. A vague "can we talk?" leaves people guessing in a similar way until the conversation happens.

faqs.q: How does unclear communication lead to office politics?
faqs.a: When clear messages are missing, people start reading signals everywhere: who was invited, who replied, how a note was worded. Information gets hoarded and interpreted. That looks like politics, but it is usually people coping with a gap where clear messages should be.

faqs.q: Isn't being blunt just as bad as being vague?
faqs.a: Blunt and clear are different things. Kim Scott's Radical Candor calls bluntness without care Obnoxious Aggression and vagueness out of niceness Ruinous Empathy. Aim for a message that names the issue, gives the reason and suggests a next step, said with respect for the person hearing it.
